title: No charges for Peel cops after shooting of man and innocent bystander
subtitle: A neighbour struck in her Mississauga kitchen took one of 19 rapid-fired bullets last March; 11 others killed Marc Ekamba-Boekwa.
article: Marc Ekamba-Boekwa was unceremoniously buried in a pauper's grave weeks after he was shot dead by Peel Regional Police officers last March, his sister told the Star.
"It seems no one cared. His life didn't matter," Sephora Ekamba, who lives in Montreal, said Thursday.

She was speaking the day after Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, announced that no criminal charges would be laid against three officers who fired a total of 19 bullets in quick succession on Queen Frederica Dr. in Mississauga the evening of March 20.
Eleven of those bullets struck Ekamba-Boekwa, 22, who the SIU says was advancing on police with a kitchen knife that had a 6-inch blade.

In an unusual move, the SIU released its findings just after 9 p.m. Wednesday, with the key information - that a man was killed and that a bystander was struck by a stray bullet in her kitchen - included much further down in its news release.

Asked why the agency released SIU director Tony Loparco's decision well after business hours, agency spokesperson Jason Gennaro said the release came out after notifying family and others affected by the shooting.
"Late in the evening, immediately after investigators notified the last person involved, the news release was issued," Gennaro said in an email.
He said that a box at the top of the web page with the release contains previous news releases indicating that the SIU was investigating a death and an injury.
"And, it should also be noted, the case is well known," he said.
Daniel Brown, Toronto director of the Criminal Lawyers' Association, said the timing of the release could be interpreted as an attempt to "sweep the decision under the rug."

Peel Regional Police will now conduct an internal review into the shooting, "as we do with all incidents that result in SIU investigations," said Peel spokesperson Daniel Richardson. Once the review is completed, it will be presented to Peel's Police Services Board.
Under Ontario's Police Services Act, the review may be made public, but critics - including the SIU's former director, Ian Scott - have said this rarely, if ever, happens.

Earlier this fall, the results of an administrative review in the high-profile fatal shooting of Jermaine Carby by a Peel police officer were not made public. The SIU cleared the unnamed police officer.
Ekamba told the Star she plans to seek legal action against the police, as does Suzan Zreik, the woman who was injured by the stray bullet, her lawyer told the Star.
"She's disenchanted with the whole process," Michael Moon said.
Ekamba claims she and her three siblings weren't officially notified of Ekamba-Boekwa's death until much later. She said she first learned about it through an aunt about a month after the shooting.
Gennaro, the SIU spokesman, said Ekamba-Boekwa's family members in Toronto were notified immediately after his death.
"He needed help. He didn't need to be killed," said Ekamba, who found the authorities unhelpful during the investigation into her brother's death.
She described her brother, who came to Canada from the Democratic Republic of Congo with his mother (who is not related to Ekamba) at the age of 2, as "very smiling, happy, very, very calm."
The last time Ekamba spoke with her brother was almost two years ago. She said something must have changed to make him behave in the erratic way described by authorities on the evening of March 20.
Ekamba-Boekwa was advancing on the officers after they responded to a call that his mother, Boketsu Boekwa, had allegedly threatened a neighbour with a knife, according to the SIU news release.

At one point, the release says, Boekwa struck one of the officers on the back of the head with a metal pot. She is currently facing criminal charges, including conspiring to murder a police officer and her neighbour.

In the melee of bullets that ensued, 11 struck Ekamba-Boekwa, one hit an officer who was wearing a bullet-proof vest and another struck Zreik in the back while she was cutting limes in her own kitchen.

Loparco found that the officers were "legally justified" in shooting Ekamba-Boekwa. Given that finding, he said he was "bound to conclude that there are no grounds to charge the officers with criminal offences in relation to the injuries suffered by the two others who were wounded. They were simply in the wrong place at the wrong time through no criminal fault of anyone else."
Lawyer Peter Rosenthal, who has represented families of people killed by police, questioned whether there was still a case to charge the officers for Zreik's injury.

"It is my view that the SIU director had to consider whether excessive firing by the officers was negligent," he said. "He should have considered the possibility of charging the officers with criminal negligence causing bodily harm to the bystander in her kitchen, even if they were justified in shooting the man."
